title: Sudden withdrawal of Trump’s FDA pick blindsided officials and left key senator fuming, sources say
content: Senior health officials were blindsided by the White House decision to abandon Dr. Heidi Overton, its nominee to run the Food and Drug Administration, just hours after they believed she’d finally secured enough Senate support to advance, a half-dozen people familiar with the matter told CNN. The decision late Tuesday night was so sudden that Overton’s team found out about her fate from an Axios report that some of them initially insisted had to be a mistake, two of those people said. Since then, Overton’s allies have grown convinced that the White House used the Senate uncertainties as justification to kill a candidate that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had soured on in the months since Trump first hailed her as a “ROCKSTAR” nominee. “I think she absolutely had the votes,” one of those people familiar with the matter said. “There wasn’t any indication that she had an issue.” The surprise move to pull Overton’s nomination followed days of negotiations between her team and a handful of holdout GOP senators. Her team had just made a series of concessions Tuesday afternoon to Sen. Josh Hawley to win what officials saw as the crucial final vote, the sources said. But hours after striking that deal, the White House dropped Overton’s candidacy — catching senior HHS officials off-guard and angering Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate’s health committee. Spokespeople for the White House and the Health and Human Services Department did not respond to requests for comment on the episode. Endpoints News first reported elements of the lead-up to Overton’s withdrawal. In the aftermath, Trump officials did not appear to have a plan to quickly nominate a replacement — raising the prospect that Republicans will fail to confirm a permanent FDA commissioner before handing Senate control over to Democrats in January. The multibillion-dollar agency, which is responsible for the safety of Americans’ food and prescription medicines, has not had a permanent commissioner since May. Current acting chief Kyle Diamantas has been widely expected to leave the FDA by the end of the year, three of the people familiar said. Cassidy was livid over the abrupt withdrawal, according to two of the sources, and appeared to rule out considering another nominee this year in an X post that insisted Overton would have had the votes to advance out of his committee. “Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats,” he wrote. Cassidy, who backed Kennedy’s confirmation but has since emerged as one of his chief antagonists, lost his primary election earlier this year and is leaving Congress at the end of the term. On Wednesday, he also said he would not advance the nomination for Jim O’Neill, the administration’s pick to lead the National Science Foundation, because he felt the candidate “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Kennedy when O’Neill served as a deputy at HHS. There is little expectation among administration officials that Democrats next year will support any nominee aligned with Kennedy, who they have long criticized over his anti-vaccine policies and broader stewardship of the department. Ending Overton’s nomination has stoked fresh rounds of finger-pointing that threaten to deepen existing divides within the GOP over the administration’s healthcare agenda. And it served as the latest sign that Miller plans to empower Kennedy to more freely pursue his ambitions, after months of White House efforts to effectively sideline his most divisive and politically unpopular policies. Miller, who Trump promoted to chief of staff earlier this month, is widely seen as more supportive of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” platform than former chief Susie Wiles. The HHS secretary, meanwhile, had previously clashed with Overton during her time as a senior White House domestic policy official, where she served as the main conduit between HHS leaders and top West Wing aides, the people familiar with the matter said. Over the last several months, Kennedy and his allies came to see Overton as an impediment to his agenda, with some blaming her for slowing or outright stalling a series of key policies. Overton’s defenders countered that she had been a key MAHA advocate at the White House level — and that the slowdown was driven by a broader shift in Trump’s policy priorities ahead of the midterm elections. Trump nominated Overton in August to run the FDA based in part on the endorsement of Wiles, the people familiar with the matter said. But after Trump replaced Wiles with Miller, White House discussions about the fate of Overton’s candidacy quickly intensified, the people familiar said. Trump officials debated last week and into the weekend over whether to devote political capital to her confirmation bid — or abandon her candidacy altogether. Overton’s standing was also hurt by a series of public attacks levied by former senior HHS official Calley Means, a close Kennedy ally who accused her and Wiles of prioritizing corporate interests over the MAHA agenda and blamed her for a range of the movement’s policy setbacks. The allegations gained traction within the White House, where Miller had already taken some early steps viewed as a rebuke of Wiles’ operation — including banning meetings with lobbyists on the White House grounds without prior approval. The allegations also energized opposition to Overton across the broader MAHA movement, spurring activists to urge officials in public and private to drop her nomination. “She was Susie’s person,” a person familiar with the matter said. “They were definitely rooting for her failure.” Overton and senior health officials working on her nomination had stepped up their campaign to win the sufficient Senate votes in the meantime. Overton met privately with Cassidy last week, in a sit down that her team believed locked in his support, two of the people familiar said. The senator, in his X post, later confirmed he’d planned to vote for her. Health officials had also worked to assuage the lingering concerns of senators, including GOP moderates Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins, by dispatching Medicaid and Medicare official Dr. Mehmet Oz to make calls on Overton’s behalf, two of the people said. Spokespeople for Murkowski and Collins did not respond to requests for comment. The final challenge, Overton’s team believed on Tuesday, was winning over the stridently anti-abortion Hawley. Officials ultimately made a handful of commitments that afternoon tied to the FDA’s ongoing study of mifepristone, the nation’s most-used abortion pill, including posting the study’s anticipated completion date on the agency’s website. “I thought her responses were completely responsive to everything I asked for,” Hawley told reporters on Wednesday, praising her for the “strongest commitments any nominee has made on life.” In a sign of heath officials’ confidence on Tuesday that Overton would advance through committee, they were already plotting to have her meet with another anti-abortion senator, Steve Daines of Montana, whose support she would need ahead of her final confirmation vote in the full Senate. But the White House yanked her nomination shortly afterward, abruptly ending Overton’s three-month candidacy before she could reach a single recorded vote. CNN’s Sarah Owermohle contributed to this report.

title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
content:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

title: Jimmy Dimly is back and we should treasure him while we can
content: S ooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”. As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024 . A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never heard her speak. The Tories would have done better if they had put up a turnip. This time, the Tories are determined to take themselves a little more seriously. With the emphasis on a little. Enter James Cleverly . One of this column’s favourite sons. It’s only with his reappearance that you realise quite how much you’ve missed him. James has the CV of a political heavyweight. But at heart he still is, and always will be, Jimmy Dimly. The foreign secretary who rubbished Rishi Sunak’s Rwanda plan as “bat-shit crazy” only to find himself moved sideways to home secretary where he was forced to defend and implement it. Things like this keep happening to Jimmy D. Disaster follows him around like an ultra-needy cockapoo. Yet you can’t help loving him for it. Because there’s something rather sweet about a man who takes himself quite so seriously. Never realising that the joke’s on him. People are laughing at him, not with him. A man who always seems to be living his life several sentences behind every conversation. Stuck in second gear. Someone who means well, but can’t quite keep up. We don’t know yet if Sadiq is planning to stand for a fourth term in 2028, but he may be looking at Dimly and thinking things could have been a lot worse. Inside a central London office suite on Thursday morning, Jimmy D and the two other Tory mayoral candidates, Festus Akinbusoye and Sara Gezdari, gathered to hear the results of the first round of voting. Or only round. The returning officer announced that Dimly had received 86% of the vote and was duly elected. Interestingly, we weren’t told how many people had voted. I guess it’s less embarrassing than saying Jimmy had received 43 votes. Fair to say that this is not an election that has gripped the Tory party. Nor London. No one is much interested in who is going to be runner-up again to Labour. Jimmy D gave a big smile. This was his moment and he was going to milk it. He strode to the lectern to address a largely uninterested audience. First, he wanted to thank Festus and Sara for the brilliant campaigns they had run and for the lively conversations they had sparked. “You are an asset to London and the whole country,” he said. Er … hang on a mo. What campaigns and what conversations? This was the first time most of London had heard of Festus and Sara, so it was tragic that the acclaim was for their imminent return to obscurity. “Nobody loves London more than me,” Dimly continued. So he wasn’t planning to stand again as an MP. He was all in for London. This sounded more like a man clinging to a life raft than an endorsement of the capital. In truth, he has always looked out of sorts in Kemi Badenoch’s Reform-lite Conservative party. He had been more of an old-school Tory who was never comfortable just trashing foreigners and people on benefits. So this was more a last chance of extending his political career while maintaining some self-respect rather than a statement of commitment. He might be a bit crap, but he was a bit crap with a heart. We then got five minutes of a love letter to London. “The answer to ‘why London’ is because London is London,” he said gnomically. At times like these, Dimly excels himself. We should treasure him while we still have him. London was the best city in the world. Then, as if realising he had just given a party broadcast on behalf of Sadiq, he gave us five minutes on why London was the most rubbish city in the world. Basically everything that was wrong with London was the fault of “Khan”. Jimmy couldn’t bring himself to use his first name. Everywhere you went there were people being murdered in front of your eyes and motorists had been deprived of the opportunity of driving at high speed and killing cyclists and pedestrians. Only Dimly could make London a fun place again. To all those people who had been up all night playing Grand Theft Auto VI, he was going to turn the capital into a video game. London was going to be bigger than big. So big no one would ever miss it again. Or something. There was just time for a few questions. How did he feel about having supported Truss’s mini-budget and being pro-Brexit? On the whole, Londoners weren’t that keen on either of these. Two-thirds of Londoners reckoned Brexit had been a disaster. How was he going to reconcile that one? Now Jimmy D struggled with his hearing. Turned out he couldn’t make out the Brexit word. Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion He didn’t want to talk about the past, he was the future. Except when he was talking about the Wrath of Khan. “Khan hates London,” he insisted. “What’s more Andy Burnham hates London too.” In the DimlyVerse, neither Sadiq nor Andy would be happy until the capital had been razed to the ground. What about the commitment to abandoning net zero and membership of the ECHR? Those were Kemi’s red lines. Were they his? Jimmy shuffled awkwardly and mumbled “Yes”. A lie. Dimly believes in both. As do most Londoners. There has almost certainly been a pact that Kemi will look the other way so long as Jimmy doesn’t make a big deal about the differences in their politics. Dimly just wanted to re-emphasise his commitment to London. He was all for the things that Londoners wanted. And if he wasn’t, he would do his best to pretend that he was. He couldn’t say fairer than that. “I am only going to comment on my comments,” he said in conclusion. Sometimes, it’s hard not to love him. At the very least, the next two years will be a golden time for sketch writers.
